saṃbandhinamākarṣati, sa niyatastāvat na bhavati anuktatvāt aprakaraṇāpannatvā- cceti sarva eva pratīyate | anupādānāt iti śabdena prakaraṇena vā | sarvāntarbhāvāt iti codyam | yadyasau iti siddhāntaḥ | tatra codye tāvadayamāśayaḥ-aniyatatvāt saṃbandhino nikhila eva jaḍaśca ajaḍaśca bhāvavargaḥ pratīyate | tatra ajaḍānāṃ sa ātmā caitanyalakṣaṇa ekaḥ kadācit śakyo'bhidhātum, jaḍāstu amī pṛthakparicchinnasvarūpāḥ kathamekātmānaḥ pṛthaksvabhāvānāmekasvabhāvatvavirodhāditi | uttarasya tu ayamāśayaḥ-iha svātmeti sva ātmanaḥ svasāmānyalakṣaṇārthakriyākāritvāderanyāpekṣasya saṃbandhī ātmīyo'nanyāpekṣo'naupādhiko bhavati | tatra ye jaḍāste yāvat jaḍābhimatāḥ, tāvat sadasattvamapi etairdurlabhamātmani, kā tu kathā nīlapītasukhaduḥkhāditvasya | tathāhi yaḥ svātmani san, sa yadi asan syāt, kimasya duṣyet | tathaiva arthakriyāṃ kuryāditi cet, karoti ityevaṃ yadi syāt tatkiṃ syāt | tathaiva prakāśeteti cet, prakāśamānatā kimasya svamahimā | omiti cet; mama prakāśate, caitrasya prakāśate iti kathaṃ saṃgacchatām | prātipattrī sā prakāśateti cet, pratipatturyadyasau, tat tasya sā kiṃ bhavatu | tadvaśāt sa prakāśata iti tu apūrvā yuktiḥ | evaṃ hi śvetavaśāt pītaṃ śvetate ityapi syāt | yadi asya ātmīyaṃ, tadvaśādanyatra na bhavati nīlateva pīte; tathā ca prakāśarūpatā pramāturātmīyeti (page 43) kathaṃ sā nīle bhavet | tatra bhavanasya tādātmyaṃ vyāpakamanyathā nīle'pi pītatetyādi sahasraśākhamāsamañjasyaṃ dṛśyamānatādrūpyavyāpakasya niyamasya viruddhaṃ prasajyeta | tasya tādātmyasya viruddhamanyātmatvaṃ, tadeva ca anyadīyatvam; athā anyasya tatsaṃbandhīti katham | naca idaṃ nīlādeḥ prakāśamānatvaṃ vinā kiñcit nijajīvitamastītyanapahnavanīyaprakāśamāna- tābalāt pramātṛprakāśatādātmyamasya aṅgīkāryamiti bodhātmāna eva nīlādayo'pi, natu eṣāmanyat vapuriti teṣāmapi sa eva svātmā maheśvara iti iṣṭameva | kaḥ prasaṅgārthaḥ | aniṣṭāpattirhi prasaṅgaḥ | tadetadāha āstāṃ loṣṭādiḥ iti | tasya hi sphuṭaṃ prakāśamānasya ko bodhātmatāyāṃ vivādaḥ | abhāvo'pi yastuccho na
**The own-self: the one consciousness, whose body is the world** The kārikā says that the own-self alone is the Lord. But what is this "own-self"? Does it reach the whole world — the inert things, the void, everything? The objector presses hard on this. If the maheśvara is the self of the blue, then he must be the self of the yellow too; and then how can the world be divided — "this is the blue, this is the yellow"? The answer turns on what "own-self" really means. The "own" in "own-self" (svātmā) is not restricted to anything in particular; so it is the self's own — the inner, non-other-dependent, un-conditioned relation. And what is that? It is consciousness. For the conscious things, he is plainly the one self. But for the inert — the lump of clay, the blue — how can they have one self, since separate things seem to have separate natures? Here Abhinavagupta shows that the inert, in its supposed inertia, has no real being at all. If the clay is truly in itself, is it or is it not? If it were not, nothing would suffer; if it did its effect, so what; if it shone, what is its own glory? The "it shines for me, for Caitra" fails too — for the perception belongs to the perceiver, not to the thing; and "by the perceiver it shines" is a new-fangled reason that would make the white make the yellow white. In truth, the thing has no being apart from its being-manifested; and being-manifested is the consciousness's own act. So the blue and the yellow are not things with their own separate bodies; they are *awareness-forms* (bodhātmānaḥ) — and their own-self, no less than ours, is the maheśvara. What of the void, the mere nothing? If it is cognized at all, then the maheśvara is its self too; if it is not cognized, then it is nothing, and no one's self is at issue. The test is always the same: is it cognized? That is the whole answer — the "being-cognized" is what makes anything the self of the one consciousness. And so the division of the world. If the maheśvara is the self of the blue and of the yellow alike, how is "this is the blue, this is the yellow" possible? Abhinavagupta's answer is that the division is not a division of the self. The whole known world is the *body* of the consciousness-self. Just as my body, though an object of my knowledge, is nonetheless "I" — not metaphorically, but literally, by the un-abandoned support of the self — so the whole world is "I" to the consciousness. The body's being "I" is no mere figure of speech (as when we call a tool by its owner's name); even those who think themselves quite separate from one another feel the body as "I." So the consciousness is world-form (viśvarūpā); the blue and the yellow are not cut off from it as from a thing outside, but are its very forms, as the space of the jar and the space of the cloth are the one space. The upshot: the own-self is the one consciousness, whose body is the whole world. The blue and the yellow, the inert and the void, are all awareness-forms; their own-self is the maheśvara. The division of the world is the division of what appears within the one light, not a split in the light itself. And this one — the knower, the doer, the self of all — is the Lord: the jñātṛ-kartṛ, who knows and acts, and whose very being is to be the self of everything. ---

> The kārikā says "the own-self alone" (svātmā eva) is the Lord. The objection presses on what > "own-self" includes: if the maheśvara is the self of the blue, he is equally the self of the yellow — > so how is the world divided? Abhinavagupta answers that the "own" (sva) is not restricted; the whole > being-class, inert and conscious, is related. For the inert, in their inert-ness, even being/non-being > is hard in the self: "it shines for me, for Caitra" fails, since the perception belongs to the > perceiver. Without the blue's being-manifested there is no own-life; so the blue and the rest are > awareness-forms (bodhātmānaḥ), and their own-self too is the maheśvara. > > The division of the world is then answered: all the known is the *body* (śarīra) of the > consciousness-self. As the body, though known, is "I," so the whole world is "I" to the consciousness. > The division is of what appears within that consciousness, not a division of the self itself. viśvarūpā (world-form).
